Genital Ulcer: Painless or Painful

Painless genital ulcer with a raised border in a sexually active adolescent · NBME · does the ulcer hurt, and are there vesicles or suppurating nodes?

Source vignette Pt — 17 yo F, 5 days of a nontender vulvar lesion; three male partners, condoms used inconsistently; afebrile, normal vital signs · Exam — 2 cm ulcer with raised borders on the right labium majus · Q — the most likely causal organism; options were organism classes: gram-negative bacillus, gram-negative diplococcus, obligate intracellular bacterium, protozoan, spirochete and virus
The decision point

A single painless genital ulcer with a firm, raised border and no systemic signs is a primary syphilis chancre. The cause is Treponema pallidum, a spirochete. Genital herpes and chancroid both cause painful ulcers. HSV (herpes simplex virus) starts as grouped vesicles that break into shallow ulcers. Chancroid causes deep ulcers, often with tender suppurative inguinal nodes.

A chancre can also be multiple or painful, and the exam alone often misleads. Test every genital ulcer for syphilis and HSV, and test for HIV. Early in primary syphilis the RPR (rapid plasma reagin) can still be nonreactive. Darkfield microscopy or a molecular test of the ulcer exudate detects the spirochete directly.

Genital ulcer in a sexually active patient: the differential
DiagnosisUlcerNodes and courseThe NBME tell
Primary syphilis: Treponema pallidum, a spirocheteUsually single, painless, clean base, firm raised borderPainless, rubbery inguinal nodes; heals in weeks even untreated, and secondary syphilis can followPainless ulcer with an indurated, raised border; no vesicles
Genital herpes: HSV-2 or HSV-1, a virusPainful grouped vesicles on a red base that break into shallow ulcers, then crustTender inguinal nodes; a first episode can bring fever and dysuria; recursVesicles first, painful, often multiple
Chancroid: Haemophilus ducreyi, a gram-negative bacillusOne or more deep, painful ulcers with ragged, undermined edges and a purulent baseTender suppurative inguinal nodes (buboes) that can rupture; rare in the United StatesPainful ulcer with a suppurating node
Lymphogranuloma venereum: Chlamydia trachomatis L1 to L3, an obligate intracellular bacteriumSmall papule or ulcer that heals on its own and often goes unnoticedTender, usually unilateral inguinal or femoral nodes; proctocolitis after rectal exposureThe nodes, not the ulcer, bring the patient in
Discharge infections: N. gonorrhoeae (gram-negative diplococcus), C. trachomatis (obligate intracellular), Trichomonas vaginalis (protozoan)No ulcerCervicitis, urethritis and pelvic inflammatory disease; trichomoniasis gives a frothy, malodorous dischargeDischarge without an ulcer
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Nontreponemal test (RPR or VDRL, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) plus a treponemal testFirstBoth reactiveSyphilis; a nonreactive nontreponemal test does not exclude early primary syphilis
HSV NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test, usually PCR, polymerase chain reaction) of a lesion swabFirstPositiveGenital herpes
HIV testScreenReactiveCo-infection; test everyone with a genital ulcer
Darkfield microscopy or PCR of ulcer exudateConfirmsMotile spirochetes or T. pallidum DNAPrimary syphilis, including before serology turns reactive
H. ducreyi culture on special mediaBy branchPositive in under 80%Chancroid; probable when ulcers are painful and syphilis and HSV tests are negative
Tzanck smearSkipInsensitive and nonspecificReplaced by HSV NAAT
Scenario bank
Management Primary syphilis — benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM (intramuscular) once for adults and adolescents; children get 50,000 units/kg, up to 2.4 million units · Penicillin allergy, not pregnant — doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days · Pregnancy — penicillin only; desensitize a patient with penicillin allergy, then treat · Genital herpes, first episode — oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir for 7 to 10 days · Chancroid — azithromycin 1 g orally once or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once
Organism classes Spirochete — Treponema pallidum: painless chancre · Virus — herpes simplex virus: painful vesicles, then ulcers · Gram-negative bacillus — Haemophilus ducreyi: painful ulcer, suppurative nodes · Obligate intracellular bacterium — Chlamydia trachomatis: cervicitis, or lymphogranuloma venereum with prominent nodes · Gram-negative diplococcus — Neisseria gonorrhoeae: cervicitis and discharge · Protozoan — Trichomonas vaginalis: frothy, malodorous discharge
Pearls In the United States, most genital ulcers in young, sexually active patients are genital herpes or syphilis · Treat presumptively for syphilis when the ulcer looks like a chancre, before results return · The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is fever, headache and myalgia within 24 hours of treating syphilis; it is not a penicillin allergy · How NBME framed it: every option was an organism class, so the ulcer had to be named as syphilis and then matched to spirochete.
Pairs with Part II Fever, Rash and Joint Pain in a Child or Adolescent owns secondary syphilis: is there a rash on the palms and soles? Part I Acute Cervicitis owns gonorrhea and chlamydia: is there a discharge instead of an ulcer?
Transferable rule For a genital ulcer, ask first whether it hurts. A painless, indurated ulcer is primary syphilis until proven otherwise. A painful ulcer is herpes when vesicles came first and chancroid when the inguinal nodes suppurate.
Unchecked attributeGram-negative bacillus: Haemophilus ducreyi causes a genital ulcer, but the chancroid ulcer is painful and comes with tender suppurative nodes.
Unchecked attributeVirus: HSV (herpes simplex virus) is the most common cause of genital ulcers, but its lesions are painful and start as grouped vesicles.
True-fact-wrong-slotObligate intracellular bacterium: Chlamydia trachomatis is common in sexually active adolescents, but it causes cervicitis, and its lymphogranuloma venereum strains cause only a small transient ulcer.
Salient decoyGram-negative diplococcus: multiple partners suggest gonorrhea, but gonorrhea causes cervicitis and discharge, not an ulcer.
True-fact-wrong-slotProtozoan: Trichomonas vaginalis causes a frothy, malodorous discharge with itching, not an ulcer.
